title: Linux History & What is an OS/Kernel

blocks.heading: Before Linux: Unix
blocks.body: In 1969, engineers at Bell Labs (AT&T) built an operating system called Unix. It introduced ideas that are still core to Linux today: everything is a file, small programs that do one thing well, and a hierarchical filesystem. Unix became hugely influential, but it was proprietary — companies had to pay for licenses to use or modify it.

blocks.heading: The GNU Project
blocks.body: In 1983, Richard Stallman started the GNU Project with a goal: build a completely free (as in freedom) Unix-like operating system. Over the next decade, GNU produced excellent free tools — a compiler, a text editor, a shell, and core utilities like ls, cat, and grep. But GNU was missing one critical piece: a kernel, the core program that actually talks to the hardware.

blocks.heading: Linus Torvalds and the Kernel
blocks.body: In 1991, a Finnish student named Linus Torvalds started writing his own kernel as a hobby project, posting about it on a newsgroup. That kernel became Linux. Combined with GNU's tools, it formed a complete, free operating system — technically 'GNU/Linux,' though most people just call it Linux.

blocks.heading: OS vs Kernel vs Distro
blocks.body:
These three terms get mixed up constantly:

- The KERNEL is the core program that manages hardware — memory, CPU scheduling, devices. Linux itself is only the kernel.
- The OPERATING SYSTEM is the kernel plus the tools needed to make it usable — a shell, core utilities, system services.
- A DISTRIBUTION (distro) is a complete, ready-to-install package: the Linux kernel, GNU tools, a package manager, and often a desktop environment. Ubuntu, Debian, and Fedora are all distros built on the same Linux kernel.

blocks.heading: Your First Command: whoami
blocks.body: Let's use the terminal for the first time. The 'whoami' command simply prints the username you're currently logged in as — useful for confirming who the system thinks you are.

blocks.instructions: Switch to the terminal on the right and type whoami, then press Enter.

blocks.heading: Where Am I? pwd
blocks.body: 'pwd' stands for 'print working directory.' Every terminal session has a current location in the filesystem, and pwd tells you exactly where that is.

blocks.instructions: Try pwd in the terminal. Compare it to what you saw when we looked at the filesystem earlier.
